A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same newspaper AI-use audit. Their complete 27-page contents, including figures, tables and appendices, support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V3 reports original analyses of recent_news, opinions and ai_reporters, including AI-use estimates, detector comparisons, a 100-article disclosure audit and quotation analyses.

after.justification: V4 retains the original empirical analyses and reports an expanded disclosure audit, manual factuality assessment, translation experiments and additional detector checks.

M1.justification: The core Pangram detection pipeline, three-category label mapping and QWEN3-8B topic classification remain unchanged. V4 identifies the detector version used, but does not establish a change to the underlying method; the added work consists of evaluation and analysis.

E1.justification: All three original corpora and their temporal coverage remain, with ai_reporters moved to the appendices. V4 extends assessment to direct verification of factual claims and explicitly reports a controlled translation scenario covering 12 languages; v3 mentions only an unspecified small-scale translation check.

E2.justification: GPTZero remains the comparison detector in the same balanced 1,000-article experiment, with the same confusion matrix and 88.2% agreement. GPT-4.1 supplies translations for robustness testing rather than serving as a new detection baseline.

E3.justification: The disclosure sample increases from 100 to 200 articles, and the new factuality comparison uses 100 AI-labeled and 100 human-labeled articles. Ownership analysis switches to newer Medill metadata, increasing article matching from approximately 52% to 87%. Topic-label validation changes from 500 samples in v3's main text to 100 in v4, resolving the discrepancy with v3's appendix, which already specified 100; this does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: V4 adds a manual hallucination analysis with examples, develops the briefly mentioned translation check into a documented multilingual robustness analysis, and adds temporal topic-bias testing and a pre-ChatGPT false-positive check using opinions. The existing quotation, republication and longitudinal reporter analyses are retained, largely in the appendices.

E5.justification: V4 adds Wilson confidence intervals for disclosure and historical false-positive estimates, Fisher's exact test for factuality, FDR-corrected McNemar tests for translation disagreements, and permutation chi-squared tests using 10,000 samples for topic variation. These substantially extend v3's statistical reporting; existing agreement statistics and circulation tests remain.

E6.justification: New results include hallucinations in 41% of AI-labeled versus 5% of human-labeled articles, plus translation and topic-bias findings. Table 2's allowed/prohibited/no-policy counts change from 7/2/91 to 12/2/186 under the larger disclosure sample. Updated ownership links yield revised estimates, such as Advance Publications' weather rate changing from 74.4% to 81.0%. V3's top-50 outlet results and several illustrative cases are removed or replaced. The headline 9.1% prevalence and 6.4-fold opinion/news ratio remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The existing label definitions, quotation-probability expressions and duplicate-similarity thresholds are retained. V4's additional statistical analyses introduce no new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation.

C1.justification: V4 adds the abstract and introduction claim that AI-labeled articles are 8.2 times more likely to contain hallucinated claims, extending the main contribution to factual reliability. The central prevalence, uneven adoption, opinion-writing and limited-disclosure claims remain, with more explicit qualification that authorship findings are detector outputs.

C2.justification: V4 interprets translation as generally suppressing AI detections and temporal topic differences as evidence against fixed topic-specific detector bias. It also connects detected AI use to uncorrected factual errors. New limitations identify dependence on one translation model, untested human translation and exploratory multilingual findings, while stronger qualifications distinguish detector labels from definitive authorship attribution.

D1.justification: V4 specifies Pangram v2.0 for reported results and explains that linked examples display newer v3.2 predictions. It documents the ownership metadata date and matching counts, and provides the GPT-4.1 translation prompt and paragraph-preserving 2,000-token chunking procedure. Existing scraping details and dataset/code release statements are retained.

R1.justification: V4 adds the BBC/EBU news-integrity report and a GPT-4.1 reference, while removing the Zeng et al. hybrid-authorship citation. Most related-work positioning remains unchanged. The Pangram multilingual study was already linked in v3, so its formal bibliography entry is not a newly introduced source.

P1.justification: V4 substantially restructures the narrative: the main reporter section becomes Appendix C, collection details move to Appendix A, and several analyses move to Appendix D. Main-text passages are condensed and rewritten, a prominent opening disclaimer is added, and author names in the opinion examples are replaced with professional roles. The author list and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: The ownership heatmap is revised with different owner rows and reordered topics, then displayed twice as v4 Figures 1 and 14. V4 adds hallucination and translation tables and a translation-prompt figure, removes the outlet-ranking table, API screenshots and print photograph, and shortens or relocates case tables. Many other plots are visually unchanged but relocated to the appendices.

improvement.justification: V4 strengthens the audit through additional detector checks, more complete and current ownership metadata, confidence intervals and clearer authorship qualifications. Its factuality assessment also provides evidence beyond v3's quotation-detection proxy. These gains are limited by sparse documentation of factuality sampling and annotation, and inconsistencies in new results: for example, Table 10 reports 83.0% French agreement, although its 9 false positives and 35 false negatives among 300 articles imply 85.3%. Such issues limit confidence in the added findings.
